content: Of the 53 individuals who expressed interest in the guideline for managing chronic pain in children, 49 were technical experts specializing in clinical treatment of chronic pain in children, academic researchers in this field, or addiction researchers. One applicant anticipated being an end-user of the guideline, while three others had technical expertise in related areas such as health economics, bioethics, equity, or human rights. Most submissions came from individuals working in the WHO Region of the Americas (19), the European Region (14), and the African Region (12). To incorporate additional perspectives, particularly from underrepresented regions or areas of expertise, the WHO Steering Group sought recommendations for additional individuals from relevant WHO departments and expert advisory panels. This process identified nine additional members for the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The GDG held two virtual meetings. The first, on January 24, 2020, finalized and approved the guideline's general scope, key questions, outcomes, and target audience. In a subsequent survey, GDG members prioritized potential outcomes of interest. The second meeting, held from September 14–18, 2020, involved reviewing GRADE evidence profiles, interpreting evidence on benefits, harms, and other considerations, and formulating recommendations, guiding principles, best practice statements, and a list of research gaps. A guideline methodologist was hired as a consultant to support the WHO Steering Group and GDG throughout the development process. This expert specialized in evidence synthesis, critical appraisal, GRADE methodology, and the formulation of evidence-based recommendations. Two systematic review teams were contracted by the WHO Steering Group to address key questions, perform systematic reviews, develop GRADE evidence profiles, assess the quality of evidence, and present findings to the GDG. The first review focused on the effectiveness and safety of physical, psychological, and pharmacological interventions for managing chronic pain in children. The second review synthesized qualitative evidence on the sociocultural acceptability of these interventions and the values and preferences of patients, caregivers, and providers. A consultant economist was also hired to conduct a rapid systematic review of existing economic evaluations of the interventions examined in the guideline and to provide cost data on various treatments in diverse settings. An External Review Group (ERG) provided input on the final content and presentation of the guidelines. These individuals, identified by WHO technical officers and the Steering Group, brought diverse perspectives and expertise to complement the GDG. Their role was to review the draft guideline, identify errors or missing data, and clarify issues related to implementation, dissemination, ethics, regulation, and monitoring. ERG members attended the September 2020 GDG meeting, where recommendations were formulated, and participated in discussions but did not have a direct role in formulating or approving recommendations. Representatives from pediatric, anesthesiology, palliative care, and pain organizations were invited to attend the September 2020 GDG meeting as observers. These organizations were potential end-users and implementers of the guidelines or represented target audiences. Only one invitee accepted. Observers were allowed to speak only at the explicit request of the meeting co-chairs and did not participate in formulating recommendations. The guideline was funded solely by WHO, with no external funding sources. All contributors, including GDG members, ERG members, and contractors, completed WHO declarations of interest (DOI) forms. Potential GDG members also submitted detailed curricula vitae and brief biographies, which were published for public notice and comment. No comments were received, and no significant conflicts of interest were identified. All appointed members were permitted to fully participate in the guideline development process. At the beginning of the two GDG meetings, all attendees verbally declared any relevant interests, highlighting updates. The WHO Steering Group conducted internet searches for additional information on prospective members, including research funding sources, declarations of interest, board memberships, affiliations, and publications. Financial, intellectual, and other interests were assessed for potential or perceived risks to impartiality. Management options for significant interests included conditional participation, partial exclusion, or total exclusion. No significant conflicts of interest were identified among GDG members. The GDG nominated and confirmed two co-chairs at the first meeting on January 24, 2020. These individuals were selected for their experience in managing group processes, interpreting evidence, and chairing WHO meetings requiring consensus-building among participants with diverse views. The co-chairs served as liaisons between the GDG and WHO Steering Group, facilitated discussions, and guided the consensus process. While they could express opinions, their primary role was to facilitate consensus-building. If consensus could not be reached, voting was conducted anonymously online, with an 80% approval threshold required for recommendations. All non-WHO attendees at GDG meetings signed a confidentiality undertaking to ensure that participants could speak freely and that WHO could provide clear, evidence-based recommendations. At the start of the guideline development process, responsible technical officers performed a scoping review to identify existing systematic reviews addressing the key question. Databases searched included PROSPERO, Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos, and Campbell Collaboration. None of the identified reviews were deemed sufficiently comprehensive or up-to-date to serve as the basis for formulating recommendations. WHO commissioned systematic reviews on the effectiveness, harms, and acceptability of physical, psychological, and pharmacological therapies for chronic pain in children. A qualitative evidence synthesis examined the sociocultural acceptability of these interventions and the values placed on their benefits and harms by patients, parents, caregivers, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders. Particular attention was given to capturing diverse viewpoints related to socioeconomic status, ethnicity, sociocultural factors, gender, religion, and geographical region. The GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of quantitative evidence for each critical and important outcome. Confidence in qualitative evidence was based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. These assessments were presented in GRADE evidence profiles to the GDG for discussion and recommendation formulation. The GDG formulated recommendations using evidence-to-decision frameworks during a virtual meeting.
